context: John Henry 'Doc' Holliday was a trained dentist from Georgia who moved west for the dry air. He died in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, in 1887, sober and in bed — not in a gunfight.

question: The score of *Akira* (1988) — taiko drums, throat singing, Balinese gamelan, chanting voices echoing through neon Neo-Tokyo — does not sound like a film score, because it isn't. It was performed by a Japanese collective of around 200 musicians. What was the group called?
answer: Geinoh Yamashirogumi, a long-running Tokyo musical commune
choices: Geinoh Yamashirogumi, a long-running Tokyo musical commune
The Yellow Magic Orchestra, the synth-pop trio of Ryuichi Sakamoto
Kodo, the taiko drum ensemble based on Sado Island in Japan
Shang Shang Typhoon, the Japanese world-music ensemble of the 1980s
context: Founder Tsutomu Ohashi led Geinoh Yamashirogumi as a kind of audio-anthropology project. The *Akira* soundtrack mixed Indonesian gamelan, Noh chanting and Bulgarian women's choir into something genuinely unprecedented.

question: George Lucas spent years pitching the science-fiction film that became *Star Wars* (1977). For most of the writing and pre-production phase, the project carried a slightly different working title — one that survives on early scripts and concept art. What was it?
answer: *The Star Wars* (with a definite article), or *Adventures of the Starkiller*
choices: *The Star Wars* (with a definite article), or *Adventures of the Starkiller*
*Episode IV: A New Hope* (which was added only after the 1981 re-release)
*Galactic Civil War*, an early treatment Lucas circulated at Universal
*The Journal of the Whills*, the title of Lucas's later expanded universe
context: Early drafts used the surname 'Starkiller' for the protagonist — later changed to Skywalker. Lucas wrote multiple drafts between 1973 and 1976; the script as filmed in 1976 had been radically simplified from earlier 200-page versions.

question: *Back to the Future* (1985) famously had to be partially refilmed five weeks into shooting. The original actor playing Marty McFly was let go and another star was brought in mid-production. Who was originally cast, and who replaced him?
answer: Eric Stoltz was originally cast; he was replaced by Michael J. Fox
choices: Eric Stoltz was originally cast; he was replaced by Michael J. Fox
Crispin Glover originally read for Marty before being moved to George
C. Thomas Howell turned the part down to do 'Soul Man' (1986)
Anthony Michael Hall turned the part down due to John Hughes commitments
context: Robert Zemeckis felt Stoltz was too serious for the comic tone. Stoltz had filmed five weeks of footage; almost none survives. Fox had to film 'BTTF' nights while shooting 'Family Ties' days for nearly nine months.

question: *Ghostbusters* (1984), directed by Ivan Reitman, was written by two of its three lead actors. The third lead — Bill Murray — joined late. Which two co-stars wrote the screenplay, in addition to acting in it?
answer: Dan Aykroyd and Harold Ramis (with Aykroyd writing the original screenplay)
choices: Dan Aykroyd and Harold Ramis (with Aykroyd writing the original screenplay)
Bill Murray and John Belushi, before Belushi's death cancelled Belushi's role
Rick Moranis and Sigourney Weaver, who first met as Columbia University students
Eddie Murphy and Ernie Hudson, before Murphy stepped away for 'Beverly Hills Cop'
context: Aykroyd's original screenplay involved ghostbusting teams in alternate dimensions — a hugely more expensive concept than the final film. Ramis pulled it back to a single team operating out of a Manhattan firehouse with one car.

question: *Terminator 2: Judgment Day* (1991) by James Cameron introduced the T-1000, an upgraded liquid-metal Terminator that could change shape. The effect required a combination of two visual techniques. Which two?
answer: Practical prosthetic effects combined with early computer-generated imagery
choices: Practical prosthetic effects combined with early computer-generated imagery
Stop-motion miniature work combined with deep-fake digital prosthetic effects
Hand-drawn 2D animation combined with then-new digital camera tracking
Mirror-image trick photography combined with classic prosthetic makeup work
context: Industrial Light & Magic delivered 39 CG shots — short, expensive, and groundbreaking. They cost more per minute than any prior film. The same techniques would underpin the original 1993 *Jurassic Park* a year and a half later.

question: *Trigun*'s protagonist Vash the Stampede is a wandering, nominally pacifist gunman on the desert planet Gunsmoke. He carries an enormous bounty on his head — the highest in the planet's history. What is the dollar amount of his bounty, in the show's currency?
answer: 60 billion double-dollars, called 'sixty billion double dollars' in the show
choices: 60 billion double-dollars, called 'sixty billion double dollars' in the show
10 trillion double-dollars, an inflation-era figure from the manga's later chapters
100 thousand double-dollars, a typical bounty figure for the desert setting
1 million double-dollars, the standard wandering-gunman bounty on Gunsmoke
context: The bounty bridges the comic and tragic tones of the manga: Vash is presented as a goofy hero, but the size of the bounty hints at a long, world-shaping past. Yasuhiro Nightow drew the manga from 1995 to 2007 across two phases.

question: Monkey D. Luffy, the captain of the Straw Hat Pirates in *One Piece*, possesses a rubber-like Devil Fruit power. He can stretch his limbs and entire body. What is the formal Japanese name of his Devil Fruit?
answer: Gomu Gomu no Mi, the Rubber-Rubber Fruit (a Paramecia-class fruit)
choices: Gomu Gomu no Mi, the Rubber-Rubber Fruit (a Paramecia-class fruit)
Mera Mera no Mi, the Flame-Flame Fruit (a Logia-class fruit Ace later eats)
Hito Hito no Mi, the Human-Human Fruit (Chopper's fruit, a Zoan class)
Pika Pika no Mi, the Light-Light Fruit (Kizaru's fruit, a Logia class)
context: Devil Fruit eaters lose the ability to swim. There are roughly 200 known Devil Fruits in the manga, divided into Paramecia, Zoan, and Logia. The Gomu Gomu no Mi has hidden facets later in the manga, but no spoilers here.

question: In *Demon Slayer*, the Demon Slayer Corps uses styles called 'Breathing Techniques', each derived from the original Sun Breathing and each tied to a Hashira (Pillar). Tanjiro's family style is Water Breathing, but he later integrates a much rarer style. What is the original style called?
answer: Sun Breathing, the parent style from which all others derive
choices: Sun Breathing, the parent style from which all others derive
Moon Breathing, the corrupted style used only by demons after the corps' founder fell
Wind Breathing, Sanemi Shinazugawa's style, one of the standard six
Stone Breathing, Gyomei Himejima's style, one of the standard six
context: Sun Breathing was the style of Yoriichi Tsugikuni, the strongest demon slayer in history. The various standard styles (Water, Flame, Wind, Stone, Thunder, etc.) were all developed by his students as approximations of Sun.

question: Osamu Tezuka — Japan's 'God of Manga' — established many of the modern manga conventions starting with his 1947 short-story collection. His most famous early hero, a robot boy with rocket feet, made his debut in 1952. What is the character called?
answer: Astro Boy (Tetsuwan Atom, 'Mighty Atom' in Japan)
choices: Astro Boy (Tetsuwan Atom, 'Mighty Atom' in Japan)
Black Jack, the unlicensed surgeon Tezuka introduced in 1973
Phoenix (Hi no Tori), the long-running mythological cycle from 1954
Princess Knight (Ribon no Kishi), the cross-dressing princess from 1953
context: Tezuka founded Mushi Production in 1961 and launched the *Astro Boy* anime in 1963 — the first weekly Japanese animated TV series, a model that defined the entire anime industry's broadcast economics for decades.

question: *ThunderCats* (1985-89) premiered with a 5-part pilot in syndication. The first part, sometimes aired as a TV movie depending on the market, depicted Thundera's destruction and the Thundercats' escape. What was the title of the first part?
answer: 'Exodus' — the title of the show's first episode, by writer Leonard Starr
choices: 'Exodus' — the title of the show's first episode, by writer Leonard Starr
'Lord of the Snows' — actually a later season-1 episode, not the pilot
'The Astral Prison' — also a later season-1 episode, not the pilot
'Sword of Omens' — never actually used as an episode title in the show
context: Lion-O was an adult mind in a child's body trapped in a 'suspension capsule' too small for him; his physical growth happened during the ten-year flight to Third Earth. The dynamic of an immature character in a hero's body became a recurring trope.

question: *Mortal Kombat* (1992) introduced a game mechanic that became its calling card: after a fight, a winner could perform a special finishing move on the dazed loser. What was this called, and how was it executed?
answer: A 'Fatality' — performed with a specific input sequence in the final round
choices: A 'Fatality' — performed with a specific input sequence in the final round
A 'Brutality' — actually introduced two games later in 'Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3'
A 'Friendship' — actually introduced one game later in 'Mortal Kombat II'
A 'Babality' — actually introduced one game later in 'Mortal Kombat II'
context: The Fatalities (especially Sub-Zero's spine-rip) drew Congressional attention to violent games and led to the 1994 ESRB rating system. Brutalities, Friendships, and Babalities came later as variant finishers, each with their own input combinations.

question: *NBA Jam* (1993), Midway's 2-on-2 arcade basketball game, had the famously elastic announcer voice yelling 'HE'S ON FIRE!' when a player hit three shots in a row. Who provided the voice?
answer: Tim Kitzrow, a Chicago actor who voiced most early Midway sports games
choices: Tim Kitzrow, a Chicago actor who voiced most early Midway sports games
Bill Walton, the basketball commentator and former NBA player
Marv Albert, the NBA broadcaster widely associated with NBA on NBC
Hank Williams Jr., the country singer of 'Monday Night Football'
context: Kitzrow's other NBA Jam catchphrases include 'BOOMSHAKALAKA!' for backboard-shattering dunks. He voiced *NBA Hangtime*, *NFL Blitz*, *NHL Hitz*, and reportedly recorded all 600+ NBA player name pronunciations for *NBA Jam* in a one-week session.

question: *Super Mario Bros.* (1985) contains one of the most famous glitches in console history. By performing a specific sequence of moves in the pipe area at the end of World 1-2, players can clip through the wall and reach a level the game itself never intended to exist. What is this level called?
answer: The Minus World — actually World 36-1 (often written as -1) with infinite water
choices: The Minus World — actually World 36-1 (often written as -1) with infinite water
World 8-4, the final level of the game, reached through any of the warp pipes
World 1-3, an early skip-level reachable via the World 1-2 warp pipe set
World 0-0, a developer's debug menu accessible from the title screen
context: The Minus World is a hex display artifact: the game cannot find a valid level there and loops World 2-2 (water level) indefinitely. The American 'Minus World' is just one warp pipe; the Famicom Disk System version had different glitched levels in similar exploits.

question: *Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade* (1989) cast a real-life screen legend as Indy's father, Professor Henry Jones Sr. — a perfect casting choice given the actor had played a similar adventurer role for decades. Who?
answer: Sean Connery, then 58, in a role written specifically for him
choices: Sean Connery, then 58, in a role written specifically for him
Charlton Heston, then 65, who instead starred in 'True Lies' as Helen's father
Burt Lancaster, then 75, who was approached but declined the role
Christopher Plummer, then 59, who would later star in 'Knives Out'
context: Steven Spielberg and George Lucas had wanted Connery from the early treatment phase, hoping to harness the Bond echo. Connery rewrote much of his dialogue on set; many of Henry Jones Sr.'s most-quoted moments — 'this is intolerable!' — were Connery improvisations.

question: Casper the Friendly Ghost was created in the early 1940s but didn't appear in animated cartoons until 1945, when Paramount's Famous Studios began the *Noveltoons* series. Casper appeared in *The Friendly Ghost* (1945). What ghost-physics is established in the original cartoon?
answer: Casper is a child ghost who can choose between scaring or being friendly
choices: Casper is a child ghost who can choose between scaring or being friendly
Casper haunts a single Massachusetts mansion and cannot leave its grounds
Casper is the ghost of an animal — a cat — not a child in the original
Casper has been a ghost for over a century and can travel through time
context: Joe Oriolo and Seymour Reit are credited as the original 1939 children's-book authors of Casper. Harvey Comics licensed the character in 1949 for comic books. The 1995 live-action *Casper* film starring Christina Ricci updated the character's lore considerably, including by addressing how he died.

question: Robert E. Howard's Kull of Atlantis (1929) was an exiled prince who became king of the much-later Valusian throne. His stories were typically grim, philosophical, and contemplative — a contrast to Conan's later barbarian-vigor mode. What is the iconic Kull line that has become a Howard quotation?
answer: 'For an instant, I was free' — a reflection on Kull's escape from a mirror trap
choices: 'For an instant, I was free' — a reflection on Kull's escape from a mirror trap
'By Crom!' — actually a Conan oath, not a Kull statement
'I have not yet begun to fight!' — actually a John Paul Jones naval quotation
'Death before dishonor!' — a generic phrase not associated with Kull
context: Howard wrote about a dozen Kull stories; only three were published in his lifetime. Marvel Comics adapted Kull into a series starting in 1971 (*Kull the Conqueror*). The 1997 film *Kull the Conqueror* (with Kevin Sorbo) was originally developed as a Conan film before being switched.

question: Dashiell Hammett's *The Maltese Falcon* — the detective novel introducing Sam Spade — was serialized in *Black Mask* magazine in 1929-30 before being published as a novel. Where was Spade based?
answer: San Francisco, where the entire novel's action takes place around the bay
choices: San Francisco, where the entire novel's action takes place around the bay
Los Angeles, where Raymond Chandler's Philip Marlowe was actually based
New York, where most of Hammett's earlier 'Continental Op' stories were set
Chicago, where pulp writer Carroll John Daly's Race Williams was based
context: Hammett had been a Pinkerton detective in San Francisco before turning to writing — his novels' realism came from direct experience. The 1941 Bogart-Huston *Maltese Falcon* film is the third (and best-known) adaptation. Hammett wrote five novels total before health issues curtailed his output.

question: Raymond Chandler's Philip Marlowe — the Los Angeles private detective who narrates his cases in cynical, lyrical first-person — debuted in *The Big Sleep* (1939). Marlowe was an evolution of two earlier characters Chandler had written in his *Black Mask* short stories. Where did Chandler train as a writer?
answer: On the job — after 1932 he taught himself by analyzing 'Black Mask' stories
choices: On the job — after 1932 he taught himself by analyzing 'Black Mask' stories
At Yale, where he studied English literature before turning to detective fiction
In London, where Chandler was a journalist before moving to America
Through correspondence with Hammett, who actually never coached Chandler
context: Chandler was 44 when he sold his first short story to *Black Mask*. He had been an oil-company executive in LA before being fired during the Depression. His novels — *The Big Sleep* (1939), *Farewell, My Lovely* (1940), *The Long Goodbye* (1953) — were written over a 25-year career.

question: Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer — the most violent and most popular detective character of the 1940s and 1950s — debuted in *I, the Jury* (1947). Spillane wrote rapidly and at one point claimed seven of the top ten bestselling novels of the postwar decade. How many Hammer novels did Spillane publish in his lifetime?
answer: 13 Hammer novels — with additional posthumous works completed by Max Allan Collins
choices: 13 Hammer novels — with additional posthumous works completed by Max Allan Collins
30 Hammer novels — a much larger output than Spillane actually produced
5 Hammer novels — fewer than Spillane actually published before his death
20 Hammer novels — including 'The Erection Set' (a real Hammer novel)
context: Spillane wrote the early Hammer novels in nine-day bursts. *Kiss Me, Deadly* (1952) is widely cited as the most stylish in the series; Robert Aldrich's 1955 film adaptation is now considered film noir at its sharpest. Spillane died in 2006; Collins has continued completing Spillane's unfinished manuscripts.

question: Sir Thomas Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* — the 1485 prose compilation of Arthurian romances that became the foundational English source for the entire Arthurian tradition — was printed by William Caxton at Westminster. Malory wrote most of it in prison. What was his crime?
answer: Various charges including rape, robbery, and church-pillaging in the 1450s
choices: Various charges including rape, robbery, and church-pillaging in the 1450s
Heresy, for which he was condemned by ecclesiastical court in 1471
Treason against Edward IV during the Wars of the Roses fighting
Murder of a fellow knight in a duel that the king refused to pardon
context: Most scholars now identify the author as Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel (1416-1471), who was repeatedly imprisoned. He wrote much of *Morte* during his imprisonment in Newgate. Caxton printed the work in 1485 — fourteen years after Malory's death — and gave it the French-language title we still use.

question: The Dyatlov Pass incident — the unexplained 1959 deaths of nine Soviet hikers in the northern Ural Mountains — has been the subject of every major conspiracy theory for sixty years. The hikers fled their tent at night without proper clothing in deep cold. What date and approximate location?
answer: February 1-2, 1959, on Kholat Syakhl ('Dead Mountain') in the northern Urals

January 20-21, 1958, the year before the actual incident date

question: The DB Cooper case got a tantalizing piece of physical evidence in 1980, nine years after the hijack: an eight-year-old boy named Brian Ingram found a stack of degraded $20 bills along the bank of the Columbia River. How much money was found?

question: Jack the Ripper — the unidentified serial killer who murdered at least five women in the Whitechapel district of London's East End — operated in the autumn of 1888. The five 'canonical' victims have been agreed on by Scotland Yard's contemporary detectives. Who was the first?

question: Easter Island's massive moai statues — the famous stone heads, of which there are 887 known — were carved by the Rapa Nui people between roughly 1250 and 1500 AD. Magnetic levitation using natural lodestone deposits found on the island
context: Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo's 2012 *Journal of Archaeological Science* paper demonstrated the 'walking' technique with a 5-ton replica statue, three rope teams, and 18 people. The technique matches Rapa Nui oral tradition ('the moai walked'). The 'rolling on logs' theory is largely abandoned by modern Rapa Nui archaeologists.

question: Stonehenge — the megalithic monument on Salisbury Plain in southwest England — uses two main types of stone. The huge sarsen stones are local Wiltshire sandstone. The smaller inner-circle bluestones come from a specific location much farther away. Where?

Some theories propose human transport on rafts and rollers (5,000 years ago); others propose glacial transport during the last ice age (rejected by current geological consensus).

question: The Wow! Signal — a strong narrowband radio signal received by the SETI Big Ear telescope at Ohio State University on August 15, 1977 — has never been satisfactorily explained. Astronomer Jerry Ehman wrote 'Wow!' on the printout, giving the signal its name. How long did it last?

A 2017 paper proposed comet 266P/Christensen as the source, but this has been contested. The signal has never been reobserved despite many follow-up attempts.

question: The Rake — the gaunt, pale, naked humanoid that crouches on all fours, watches sleepers, and may attack — is one of the most-cited modern internet creepypasta creatures. question: The Lincoln-Kennedy assassinations are sometimes compared via a long list of coincidences (both were succeeded by Vice Presidents named Johnson, both were elected to Congress 100 years apart, etc.). What is the most-cited specific name coincidence between the two assassins?

question: Module S2: *White Plume Mountain* (1979) by Lawrence Schick is the second 'S-series' module. It features three legendary weapons (Wave, Whelm, Blackrazor) lost to a wizard's mountain stronghold. What is unusual about its design philosophy?

question: The bulette ('landshark') — D&D's burrowing armored monster — has the same toy-store origin as the owlbear. It was based on one of the Hong Kong plastic figures Gary Gygax bought at a dime store. What dinosaur did the original toy roughly resemble?

question: Tiamat — D&D's chromatic dragon-goddess, a five-headed dragon with one head of each chromatic dragon type (red, black, blue, green, white) — debuted in *Supplement IV: Gods, Demigods & Heroes* (1976). Tiamat's good counterpart in D&D is Bahamut, the platinum dragon — a name borrowed from Arabic mythology.

question: The lich — D&D's archetypal undead wizard, who has prolonged life beyond death by binding their soul to a magical phylactery — first appeared in *Monster Manual* (1977). What is the only way to permanently destroy a lich?

Capture the lich and place them inside a magical anti-magic field forever
context: The phylactery is a small container — typically a small box, amulet, ring, or carving. Killing the lich's body without destroying the phylactery merely sends the soul back to the phylactery, where it can rebuild a new body over time. Acererak (from Tomb of Horrors) is the most-famous D&D lich; later progressing to demilich form.

question: Counterspell — a 2-mana instant that counters target spell — is Magic's iconic Blue control card from Alpha onward. The simple two-word effect ('Counter target spell') became one of the most-printed Magic cards. Who painted its iconic original art?

question: Magic's 'summoning sickness' rule prevents creatures from attacking or tapping for mana on the turn they enter the battlefield. The rule was designed to prevent infinite combos and 'free' attacks. When does a creature lose summoning sickness?

question: Area 51 — the U.S. Air Force's classified testing facility in southern Nevada — was an open secret for decades before being officially acknowledged in 2013 (via a FOIA-released CIA document). What is the facility's official name and location?

question: *Pong* (1972) — Atari's first arcade game and one of the founding video games of the entire industry — was inspired by a tennis game on the earlier Magnavox Odyssey home console. Atari's co-founder asked an engineer to design a similar simple tennis game. Who?

question: The 1977 *Monster Manual* was TSR's first hardcover publication and the first of the three Advanced Dungeons & Dragons core rulebooks. Why was the hardcover format unusual for the time?

question: *Super Mario 64* (1996) used the Nintendo 64 controller's unusual three-handle design, with the analog stick at the center. The C-buttons (yellow) on the right of the controller had a specific use in *Super Mario 64*. What was it?

question: Clark Ashton Smith's far-future Mars cycle — distinct from his Zothique (dying Earth) and Hyperborea (pre-Ice Age) cycles — was set on a planet called Xiccarph. What was unusual about the Xiccarph setting?

question: Magic's color pie has five distinct philosophical positions, each with characteristic mechanical strengths. White is the color of law, peace, and order. What is each of the other four colors associated with?

question: Robert E. Howard's last days in June 1936 were defined by his mother Hester's terminal cancer. On June 11, 1936, Hester slipped into a final coma. Howard, who had nursed her for years, walked to his car and made what fateful decision?

question: H.P. Lovecraft's most famous story, The Call of Cthulhu, was first published in Weird Tales in February 1928. The story is structured as a three-part archival document. Cthulhu himself is described as having three distinct anatomical features at one point. What are the features?

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's Tarzan of the Apes was first serialized in All-Story Magazine in October 1912. The novel introduced the Lord Greystoke who was raised by great apes in the African jungle. What was Burroughs's day job at the time he wrote the first Tarzan novel?

question: Raymond Chandler's first novel The Big Sleep (1939) introduced detective Philip Marlowe. The book established the Marlowe template — cynical, witty, working-class private eye in 1930s-40s Los Angeles. Chandler's previous career had been what?

question: J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit was published in September 1937 by Allen & Unwin in London. Tolkien wrote the book partly for his own children. The publisher's young son test-read it before publication. Who was the young reader?

question: Michael Moorcock's Elric of Melnibone first appeared in The Stealer of Souls (1961) in Science Fantasy magazine. The albino prince of decadent Melnibone wields a sentient soul-drinking sword called Stormbringer. The series is part of a larger meta-concept. What's the meta-concept?

question: Edgar Allan Poe (1809-1849) is widely credited as the inventor of the modern short story, the detective story, and the gothic horror tale. His final years were beset by poverty and addiction. He died in mysterious circumstances. What was the cause?

question: Edgar Allan Poe's 1842 story The Pit and the Pendulum is set during the Spanish Inquisition. The narrator is sentenced by an inquisitorial court and finds himself in a dungeon. Two threats menace him in turn. What are they?

question: Edgar Allan Poe's most famous poem, The Raven, was published in 1845. The 18-stanza poem features a refrain that becomes more ominous with each repetition. What is the iconic refrain?

question: William Hope Hodgson (1877-1918) was a British weird-fiction author who died in WWI's Battle of Ypres. His 1912 novel The Night Land is a vast post-apocalyptic fantasy set in a far future after the sun has died. The setting is which?

question: Asterix the Gaul, written by Rene Goscinny and drawn by Albert Uderzo, first appeared in 1959 in the French magazine Pilote. The series is set in 50 BCE Gaul. The villagers have a magical drink that gives them superhuman strength. What is the drink?

question: MAD Magazine, founded by Harvey Kurtzman in 1952 and published by EC Comics's William M. Gaines, featured its iconic gap-toothed cover boy on most covers since 1955. The character had been a stock public-domain illustration for decades before MAD adopted him. What is his name?

question: H.P. Lovecraft's The Call of Cthulhu (1928) contains one of the most-quoted passages in horror literature — a couplet supposedly from the Necronomicon describing Cthulhu's resting state. What is the famous couplet?

question: Edgar Allan Poe (1809-1849) wrote his most-anthologized horror story in 1843. The narrator describes murdering an old man, hiding his body under the floorboards, and then confessing because he believes he can hear the dead man's heart beating. What is the story?

question: Edgar Allan Poe's The Fall of the House of Usher (1839) is set in a decaying ancestral mansion belonging to Roderick Usher. The story is famous for the symbolic identification of the family with the literal house. What happens to the house at the end?

question: Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings was originally published as three volumes (1954-55). Tolkien himself preferred to call it a single novel divided into six books, not a trilogy. question: Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968) features a test that distinguishes androids from humans. The test measures empathic response to questions about the treatment of animals. What is the test called?

question: On December 5, 1945, five U.S. Navy Avenger torpedo bombers from NAS Fort Lauderdale (designated Flight 19) disappeared on a routine training mission over the Atlantic. The flight leader was Lieutenant Charles Taylor. What happened next that compounded the tragedy?

question: The Flannan Isles Lighthouse, on the Outer Hebrides off Scotland's west coast, was attended by three keepers who all vanished sometime between December 7 and 15, 1900. A relief ship found the lighthouse empty. What was found inside the lighthouse?

question: On December 1, 1948, the body of an unidentified man was found on Somerton Beach in Adelaide, Australia. A piece of paper sewn into his trouser pocket read Tamam Shud (Persian: 'It is ended'). The phrase came from a specific book. What was the book?

question: Gobekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey is a complex of megalithic stone enclosures with carved T-shaped pillars depicting animals. The site dates to roughly when?

question: On June 30, 1908, an enormous explosion occurred over the Stony Tunguska River basin in central Siberia. The blast flattened approximately 2,000 square km of forest. No impact crater was ever found. What is the leading scientific explanation?

question: Betty and Barney Hill claimed they were abducted on September 19, 1961 while driving home through New Hampshire's White Mountains. The case became the first widely-publicized alien-abduction account. Their hypnosis sessions revealed a now-famous detail of the encounter. What?

question: Lizzie Borden was charged with the August 4, 1892 axe-murders of her father Andrew and stepmother Abby Borden in Fall River, Massachusetts. The trial in June 1893 ended in her acquittal. What was the famous schoolyard rhyme about the case?

question: Easter Island (Rapa Nui) has about 900 monumental statues (moai) carved from volcanic tuff. The statues weigh up to 80 tons. How the Rapa Nui moved them from the quarry has been long debated. In 2012, an experimental-archaeology team demonstrated a feasible method. What did they show?

question: Stonehenge in Wiltshire, England, is a megalithic monument constructed from about 3000 to 2000 BCE. question: Atlantis is a mythical island described in Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias (c. 360 BCE). Plato claimed Atlantis was an aggressive Atlantic-Ocean empire that sank in a single day and night about 9,000 years before his time. Plato's character Critias attributes the story to whom?

question: The Isdal Woman is the name given to a still-unidentified woman whose body was found on November 29, 1970 in the Isdalen Valley near Bergen, Norway. The woman appeared to have been in fire and was wearing only partial clothing. Her case is famous for what specific feature?

question: Edward V, age 12, and his younger brother Richard, age 9, were placed in the Tower of London in spring 1483 by their uncle Richard, Duke of Gloucester (later Richard III). The boys were never seen again in public after that summer. What is the most widely-accepted explanation?

question: JonBenet Ramsey, age 6, was found dead in the basement of her family's Boulder, Colorado home on December 26, 1996. Acid (line shape) plus repulsion gas (cone shape); not actually the Gold Dragon's breath.
context: Gold Dragon: Fire (line) and Weakening Gas (cone). Silver: Cold and Paralyzing Gas. Bronze: Lightning and Repulsion Gas. Copper: Acid and Slow Gas. Brass: Fire (line) and Sleep Gas. Each metallic has two breath weapons.

question: Bahamut is the Platinum Dragon, the chief deity of the metallic dragons in D&D. Bahamut is lawful good and the patron of justice. Bahamut has seven golden dragon companions. Who are the seven?
answer: Seven great gold dragons who are also Bahamut's avatars; they accompany him on missions across the planes.

Twelve great wyrms (one for each calendar month); not actually Bahamut's companion count.
context: Bahamut's seven gold dragon companions appear in various adventures and lore. Bahamut himself appears as an old man with seven dogs (his companions in human form). Bahamut is sometimes called the King of the Good Dragons.

question: Tiamat is the Chromatic Dragon, the chief deity of the chromatic dragons in D&D. Tiamat has five heads, one for each chromatic color. She is lawful evil and the queen of all evil dragons. What is Tiamat's primary plane of residence?
answer: Avernus, the first layer of the Nine Hells (Baator); Tiamat rules her own domain there.

Carceri, the prison-plane; not Tiamat's primary residence despite her evil alignment.

question: Chaosium published RuneQuest in 1978, an alternative RPG to D&D. The game is set in the world of Glorantha, created by Greg Stafford. Glorantha is a distinctive setting with bronze-age fantasy and mythological depth. What's the iconic Gloranthan element?
answer: Runes (cosmic-magical letters); characters gain magic through their runic affiliations and worship.
choices: Runes (cosmic-magical letters); characters gain magic through their runic affiliations and worship.
Polychrome dragons; the world has dozens of colored dragons in a strict hierarchical system.
Industrial cities; Glorantha has a steam-punk industrial level not actually present in the setting.
Christianity (the dominant religion); Glorantha actually has no Christianity in its setting at all.
context: Runes are central to RuneQuest's magic and cosmology. Greg Stafford's Glorantha is one of fantasy's deepest worlds. RuneQuest 7e was a Kickstarter-funded revival in 2017-18.

question: Gerald Brom (often known simply as Brom) was the lead artist of TSR's Dark Sun setting (1991 onward). His painted style — dark, intense, with a heavy chiaroscuro — defined the setting's aesthetic. What was Brom's signature subject matter?
answer: Lean, hairless, often nude or semi-nude characters in extreme physical and emotional postures; deep psychological intensity.
choices: Lean, hairless, often nude or semi-nude characters in extreme physical and emotional postures; deep psychological intensity.

context: Brom's lean / nude / chiaroscuro style is unmistakable. He left D&D in the late 1990s but his Dark Sun work remains iconic. He has illustrated his own novels (The Plucker, The Child Thief).

question: Dark Sun's setting on Athas features many unusual races. One iconic Athasian race is the thri-kreen — bipedal mantis-folk who are excellent psionic warriors. What is the thri-kreen's most-distinctive racial trait?
answer: Four arms (two upper combat-arms and two lower-grasping arms); they can wield multiple weapons.

Shapeshifting (the thri-kreen can change form); allowing them to infiltrate other races easily.

question: The Forgotten Realms is set on the planet Toril. The most-detailed continent is Faerun, which contains the Sword Coast, the Heartlands, the North, and many other regions. Faerun has been compared to a European-fantasy continent. What's the most famous city in Faerun?
answer: Waterdeep, the City of Splendors, is the largest and most-famous city on the Sword Coast.

question: Greyhawk's central city (The Free City of Greyhawk) is the player-character starting hub for Gygax's home campaign. The city is on the Selintan River in central Flanaess. The city had several major guilds and factions. What was the most powerful guild?
answer: The Thieves' Guild, called the Beggars' Union in some references; a major political force in Greyhawk.

question: MTG's Drudge Skeletons (Alpha, 1993) is a low-cost black creature with a unique ability — for one black mana, the player can regenerate it after damage. The card became iconic for its 'never dies' role-playing reputation. What's the card's stat-line?

question: MTG's Terror (Alpha, 1993) is one of black's iconic removal spells. For two mana (BB), it destroys target non-artifact, non-black creature. The card has been reprinted in many early sets. What's the card's flavor design?
answer: Destroy target non-artifact, non-black creature; black creatures are immune (color-pie consistent).

question: MTG's Giant Growth (Alpha, 1993) is one of green's iconic combat tricks. For one green mana (G), it gives target creature +3/+3 until end of turn. The card has been reprinted in many sets. What's the card's design philosophy?
answer: Green's identity is in growth and physical power; +3/+3 is a substantial combat boost for one mana.

question: MTG's Swords to Plowshares (Alpha, 1993) is one of white's iconic removal spells. For one white mana (W), it exiles target creature, and that creature's controller gains life equal to its power. The card has been Reserved-Listed. What's the design lesson?

question: Kuo-Toa are fish-folk who first appeared in Module D2: Shrine of the Kuo-Toa (1978). The Kuo-Toa worship Blibdoolpoolp, the Sea Mother. The Kuo-Toa's religion is famously bizarre. What's the most-cited unusual aspect of Kuo-Toa religion?

question: D&D's lich is a powerful undead wizard. Liches are created through complex dark magic, and their soul is contained in a phylactery — an object usually concealed in their lair. question: On the rooftop of the Bradbury Building set, the dying replicant Roy Batty delivers a now-iconic monologue ending with the line 'all those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain.' Rutger Hauer trimmed the longer scripted speech the night before shooting, cutting most of the screenplay's lines and adding one image himself. What was the image he added?

question: Paul Verhoeven's 1987 Robocop is now considered a satire classic. question: Richard Garfield earned his PhD in mathematics from the University of Pennsylvania in 1993. His doctoral thesis was on a specific branch of mathematics that informed his game design career. What was Garfield's PhD area?

question: Magic's color pie — five colors of magic, each with distinct abilities and flavor — was designed by Richard Garfield as a coherent thematic system. Blue's color identity is distinct from the other four. What does Blue represent in Magic's official color pie?

question: Hajime Isayama's Attack on Titan (manga 2009-2021) is set inside three concentric walls protecting humanity from giant humanoid creatures. The wall names follow a specific naming convention. What is the convention?

question: Warren Spector's Deus Ex (2000) at Ion Storm Austin was an immersive sim — a genre that combines first-person action with player-driven approach choices through complex systems. question: The Passenger Pigeon (Ectopistes migratorius) was once the most abundant bird in North America, with flocks numbering in the billions. question: AD&D 1st and 2nd Edition used a system called THAC0 (To Hit Armor Class 0) for combat. THAC0 was a single number per character that, when paired with a d20 roll, determined whether attacks hit. THAC0 became one of the most-criticized D&D mechanics. What was the rule?
